paras: The lynching of Huse Thompson was the killing of a Black man who was found hanging from a tree near a Black church near Robeline, Natchitoches Parish, Louisiana, on a Sunday morning in early January 1903, after he had been arrested and jailed. A coroner's jury found that he had died by hanging "at the hands of unknown parties." It drew wider notice later that month, when District Judge Porter called it murder in a charge to the Natchitoches grand jury that papers from New York to Richmond quoted.

According to The Caucasian of Shreveport, Thompson was intoxicated on the Saturday before his death and was abusive and threatening toward people on the streets of Robeline. The paper said that when an attempt was made to arrest him he went to his home, where City Marshal D. C. Keegan, who had followed him, was attacked with a knife and had his throat slashed. It added that Keegan would have been "overpowered and murdered by Thompson and his family" had several citizens not come to his rescue. This account of the fight appears only in The Caucasian, and the coverage gives no version from Thompson or his family.

Thompson was arrested and jailed, and he was lynched during Saturday night or before dawn on Sunday. On Sunday morning he was found hanging from a tree near a Black church near the town. Judge Porter's charge, as quoted by The Caucasian, added details he gave "as I am informed": about the first of the month a Black man was taken from the lock-up in Robeline, beaten "in the most inhuman manner," and strangled by hanging from a tree. Neither account names any member of the mob or says how many took part.

The coroner summoned a jury of inquest, which returned a verdict of death by hanging at the hands of unknown parties. Late in January, District Judge Porter took up the lynching in his charge to the Natchitoches Parish grand jury, noting that the victim "was not charged with that nameless crime" and declaring that "it was murder, in the sight of God and man."

A New Orleans dispatch of January 28 reported that the same charge, which also noted two men shot to death at Campti and two beaten at Clarence, called for the indictment or impeachment of justices of the peace and other officials who had failed to suppress mob violence. That dispatch said "indictments are looked for," but The Caucasian did not expect the grand jury to find a bill against anyone connected with the mobbing. No report of an arrest, indictment or trial for the killing was found.

The Caucasian first reported the killing on January 7 under the headline "A NEGRO LYNCHED" and the subhead "He Resisted Arrest and Cut the Marshal's Throat," and ran the same item again the next day. That report gave the marshal's side as fact and said Thompson "was executed according to the decree of Judge Lynch." Three weeks later the same paper praised Judge Porter's charge as "A Protest Against Lynching," while holding that there could be "no excuse for lynching except the nameless crime" and using a slur in its own editorial text.

Outside Louisiana the killing reached readers only as one line in the New Orleans wire on the judge's charge, which the New York Sun ran on January 29 under "MUST PROTECT NEGROES" and the Vermont Watchman reprinted on February 5. A shorter version of the wire in the Minneapolis Journal, headed "MOB VIOLENCE," left out the Robeline reference altogether. Editorial writers used the charge to make wider points: the New Haven Journal and Courier said that if "the white man's government" could not do better by Black people it did the white race little credit, and the Richmond Times Dispatch called Porter "a wise and courageous judge."

In the Black press, the Cleveland Gazette printed the judge's words on February 14 under the heading "Confession," followed by a Youngstown Telegram comment that the lynching of Black people meant "the white government in southern states is a failure." The Gazette item named neither Thompson nor Robeline, and no Black-press report of the killing itself was found.

reader.title: Lynching of Huse Thompson
bases: A man jailed after a fight with the town marshal was taken from the lock-up and hanged from a tree by a mob (A1, A3).

Thompson was taken from jail and hanged by 'unknown parties' whom the district judge called 'the mob' and 'lynchers' (A1, A3); the Caucasian said he was 'executed according to the decree of Judge Lynch' for the knife attack on the marshal it charged him with (A1). The papers give no head count, but both call it a mob lynching.

The Caucasian's news report (A1) and the district judge's grand jury charge, quoted in the Caucasian and carried by a separate New Orleans wire (A3, A4), independently describe a Black prisoner lynched at Robeline.
